claims.text: At stage-3 Order records a domain event in its constructor (OrderPlaced), Cancel (OrderCancelled), Ship (OrderShipped), and the three refund methods: every status change its use cases make (MarkPaid records none; no use case calls it).

At stage-3 Order is stored state-based in its orders row; RecordOrderStatusHistory writes order_status_history beside it, and the event sourcing sample lives in samples/DonHang.Samples/Samples/Design/EventSourcing/.

order-history-design.md at stage-3 weighs three options: A event sourcing for Order, B a read model updated from domain events (chosen), C reading outbox_messages; the need is one list of statuses per order, oldest first.

Option A's listed losses: every use case, query and test loading and saving Order through EF Core changes (OrderService, EfOrderRepository, order list, xmin check, outbox); a projection per query; old events readable forever; the team learns a new way to store data.
EfOrderRepository implements IOrderRepository over EF Core, and Order.Version is mapped to PostgreSQL's xmin system column as its concurrency token.
Option B: history never trails the order's state, Order does not know the table, no use case changes; cost one INSERT per status change; orders placed before stage-3 have only a placed row.
Option C is rejected: outbox rows carry what the receiving service needs (email, customer name), orders before stage-3 have none, and a screen built on them breaks when the message shape changes.

The doc chooses B and lists three reasons to revisit: the whole order at any past moment, many new read models each needing a handler, an audit proving history was never edited; then event sourcing for Order alone.
GET /api/v1/orders/{id}/history returns the order's status changes from order_status_history (IOrderHistory) and never builds an Order.
An event store only appends to a stream and never changes a saved event (as taught in design.l3.event-sourcing), while order_status_history is an ordinary table that code could update.
Event sourcing pays off when the history is business data: past states must be answered or checked later, or many read models need the same changes and should be rebuildable by replay.

With event sourcing no table holds current state: one aggregate is read by replaying or reading its stream, queries across aggregates need a read model built by an event projection; old events must stay readable; the team learns a new way to store data.
Event sourcing is chosen per aggregate: storage sits behind the code that loads and saves one aggregate, so one can be event-sourced while others stay state-based.
Having domain events makes a read model cheap, not event sourcing; event sourcing is not an audit log for free, since the log is the store and carries its costs.
At stage-3 order_status_history records status changes only; no table records changes to an order's other fields (items, customer, placed_at), which are not changed after placement.
